subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Hallucinations and delusions in schizophrenia are classified as ____ symptoms.
questions.explain: Positive symptoms are additions to normal experience, such as hallucinations and delusions.

questions.q: In Ellis's ABC model of depression, what does the 'B' stand for?
questions.explain: In the ABC model A = activating event, B = beliefs (rational or irrational), C = consequences.

questions.q: A criticism of Jahoda's 'ideal mental health' definition is that it sets such demanding standards that:
options: It cannot be applied to phobias
Almost no one would be classed as abnormal
It only works in collectivist cultures
Almost everyone would be classed as abnormal at some point
questions.explain: The criteria are so stringent that virtually everyone fails to meet them all, making 'normality' near-impossible.

questions.q: An issue when classifying abnormality in psychopathology is 'cultural relativism', which means that:
options: Judgements of abnormality depend on the cultural context
questions.explain: Cultural relativism notes that behaviour judged abnormal in one culture may be normal in another, complicating diagnosis.

questions.q: In the two-process model, a phobia is MAINTAINED because avoiding the feared object reduces anxiety; this is an example of:
questions.explain: Avoidance is negatively reinforcing because it removes the unpleasant feeling of anxiety, strengthening avoidance.

questions.q: A strength of drug therapy (SSRIs) for OCD compared with psychological therapies is that it is:
options: A permanent cure that prevents relapse
Cost-effective and non-disruptive to the patient's routine
questions.explain: Drug therapy is relatively cheap and requires little effort from the patient compared with attending therapy sessions.

questions.q: A key limitation of the 'statistical infrequency' definition of abnormality is that it:
options: Cannot be applied to any psychological characteristic
May label desirable rare traits, such as a very high IQ, as abnormal
questions.explain: Statistically rare characteristics can be positive (e.g. a high IQ), so infrequency alone does not imply a problem.

questions.q: The 'deviation from social norms' definition of abnormality is most strongly criticised because:
options: Social norms are culturally and historically relative
It relies solely on statistical cut-off points
It can only be applied to physical illness
Norms are universal and never change
questions.explain: What counts as deviant varies across cultures and eras, so the definition risks social control and lacks objectivity.

questions.q: Jahoda's 'deviation from ideal mental health' criteria include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explain: Jahoda's criteria concern positive mental health (e.g. self-actualisation, autonomy, accurate perception), not statistical rarity.

questions.q: 'Irrational beliefs' and 'selective attention' to the phobic stimulus are examples of which type of characteristic of phobias?
questions.explain: Irrational beliefs and selective attention are cognitive characteristics, relating to thought processes.

questions.q: The genetic explanation of OCD is supported by candidate genes such as the COMT and SERT genes, which are described as:
options: Polygenic, each contributing a small risk
Monogenic, causing OCD on their own
questions.explain: OCD is polygenic; genes such as COMT and SERT each contribute a small amount to overall vulnerability.

questions.q: The 'D' added to Ellis's ABC model in REBT stands for:
questions.explain: REBT extends the model with D (disputing) to challenge and replace irrational beliefs.

questions.q: SSRIs, the first-line drug therapy for OCD, work by:
options: Preventing the reuptake of serotonin, increasing its availability
questions.explain: SSRIs block the reuptake of serotonin into the presynaptic neuron, raising serotonin levels in the synapse.

questions.q: 'Validity' of a psychiatric diagnosis is most directly threatened by:
options: Comorbidity, where disorders co-occur and are hard to separate
questions.explain: Comorbidity undermines validity because overlapping symptoms make it unclear whether distinct disorders are being measured.

questions.q: 'Reliability' of a diagnostic classification system such as the DSM or ICD refers to:
options: Consistency of diagnosis between clinicians or over time
Whether it measures what it claims to measure
questions.explain: Reliability concerns consistency, e.g. inter-rater agreement and stability of diagnosis over time.

questions.q: Neural explanations of OCD implicate abnormal levels of which neurotransmitter, plus dysfunction in the frontal lobes and basal ganglia?
questions.explain: Low serotonin, along with abnormal functioning of the frontal lobes and basal ganglia, is linked to OCD.

questions.q: In CBT, the technique where a client is set tasks to gather evidence against negative beliefs is sometimes called:
options: The 'client as scientist' / behavioural experiments approach
questions.explain: CBT treats the client as a scientist, using homework and behavioural experiments to test beliefs against evidence.

questions.q: Avolition and speech poverty (alogia) in schizophrenia are examples of:
questions.explain: Negative symptoms involve a loss of normal functioning, such as avolition (reduced motivation) and speech poverty.

questions.q: A central aim of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for depression is to:
options: Use a fear hierarchy with relaxation
questions.explain: CBT works by identifying and challenging dysfunctional cognitions and testing them against reality.

questions.q: Systematic desensitisation works primarily through:
options: Counterconditioning using an anxiety hierarchy and relaxation
Flooding the patient with maximum fear at once
questions.explain: Systematic desensitisation uses counterconditioning, gradually pairing relaxation with a hierarchy of feared situations.

questions.q: According to Ellis, emotional distress (the 'C') is caused not directly by the activating event but by the person's:
questions.explain: Ellis argued it is the irrational beliefs (B) about an event, not the event itself, that produce emotional consequences.

questions.q: In Beck's cognitive theory, the 'negative triad' refers to negative views of the:
options: Self, the world and the future
questions.explain: Beck's negative triad comprises negative views of the self, the world and the future.

questions.q: The original dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia proposed that symptoms result from:
options: Hyperdopaminergia (excess dopamine activity) in subcortical areas
Low serotonin in the basal ganglia
questions.explain: The original dopamine hypothesis attributed schizophrenia to excessively high dopamine activity in subcortical regions.

questions.q: Rosenhan and Seligman's criteria (e.g. unpredictability, personal distress, observer discomfort, violation of moral standards) are signs used in which definition of abnormality?
questions.explain: These signs were proposed by Rosenhan and Seligman as indicators of failure to function adequately.

questions.q: The principle of 'reciprocal inhibition' in systematic desensitisation refers to the fact that:
options: The therapist and patient inhibit each other
Relaxation and fear cannot be experienced at the same time
questions.explain: Reciprocal inhibition means relaxation and anxiety are incompatible, so relaxation replaces the fear response.

questions.q: Obsessions and compulsions in OCD are best described respectively as:
questions.explain: Obsessions are recurrent intrusive thoughts; compulsions are repetitive behaviours performed to reduce anxiety.

questions.q: Which definition of abnormality relies on the assumption that behaviour occurring rarely within the population is abnormal?
questions.explain: Statistical infrequency defines abnormality as behaviour that lies at the statistically rare extremes of a distribution.

questions.q: Avoidance, panic and freezing in the presence of a feared object are best classified as the ____ characteristics of phobias.
questions.explain: Avoidance, panic and freezing are behavioural characteristics, i.e. ways the person acts.

questions.q: Flooding is thought to be effective because prolonged exposure leads to:
options: Extinction, as the conditioned fear response is exhausted
questions.explain: During flooding the fear response cannot be sustained, so the conditioned association is extinguished.

questions.q: According to the two-process model, phobias are first ACQUIRED through:
questions.explain: Mowrer's two-process model states phobias are acquired by classical conditioning and then maintained by operant conditioning.
